title: Home life
hook: someone asked 'A'ishah what he did at home; she said he served his family, and when the prayer came, he went to pray

segments.voice: Yesterday: the best to their families, and your line, best at home. Today, what that looked like on an ordinary day.

A question put to 'A'ishah, and kept in Sahih al-Bukhari. Someone asked her what the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, used to do in his house. Not in the mosque. Not on the battlefield, not on the pulpit. In the house. It's the kind of thing you'd only ask the person who lived with him. Her answer is short. He used to be busy serving his family, she said, and when the time for prayer came, he went out to the prayer. No speech. A man at home doing the work of the home, until the call came.
screen: `WHAT DID HE DO AT HOME?` → `ASK THE ONE WHO LIVED WITH HIM.` → `SERVING HIS FAMILY.`

segments.voice: Look at the order in her answer: first the family, then the prayer. Not because the prayer mattered less. When its time came, he went, and the serving stopped. But until then, the house had his hands. The word in the Arabic report is mihnah, the work of the household, the everyday labor of a home. Other reports fill in the picture. In one kept in the Musnad of Ahmad, 'A'ishah is asked again, and she says, in paraphrase, that he mended his own clothes, repaired his own sandal, and did what any man does in his house. A man the Qur'an calls a messenger, sewing a torn garment himself. Now put that next to yesterday's hadith: the best of you are the best to their families. The serving is what that sentence looks like on a Tuesday. A shirt. A sandal strap. Whatever needs doing. And the second half of her answer keeps the serving from swallowing everything. The home was not a reason to miss the prayer, and the prayer was not a reason to skip the home. Some readers hear in this a rhythm for a whole life: the small work of love, then the turn toward Allah, then back again. The house and the prayer aren't rivals. They take turns. The prayer, when he left for it, was not an escape from the dishes. It was the next thing in the same day.
screen: `FIRST THE FAMILY, THEN THE PRAYER.` · `MIHNAH, THE WORK OF THE HOUSE.` · `HE MENDED HIS OWN CLOTHES.` · `THE HOUSE AND THE PRAYER TAKE TURNS.`

segments.voice: Let your mind walk through the place you live: the sink, the laundry, the thing that's been broken for a week. Pick one small job you'd normally leave for someone else, and see yourself doing it start to finish, without telling anyone. Then see yourself turning toward the next thing in your day; if you pray, let that be the next prayer, whenever its time comes.
Home life. In 'A'ishah's answer: he served his family, mended his clothes, and when prayer came, went to pray. Today's word.
Your line: serve, then pray. A sandal strap, and then the call. Rest well.

howItsDone: Muslims point to 'A'ishah's description of the Prophet at home, serving his family and mending his own clothes, as a model for household life, and to his going out when the time for prayer came.

chat.says: What did the Prophet actually do at home? Was he just praying all day?
options: He served his family and mended his clothes, then went out when prayer came.
He left the housework to others, so he could stay at the mosque all day.
He stayed home with the chores and often let the prayer time pass by.
